newsitem.title: USA: IBM, Intel vie with startups in Internet technology.
newsitem.headline: IBM, Intel vie with startups in Internet technology.

text.p: Dozens of companies, ranging from tiny startups to industry titans IBM Corp. and Intel Corp., are vying for the spotlight in showing off Internet products this week.

David Coursey's Internet Showcase, a three-day conference presented by Upside magazine starting Monday, will highlight upcoming products ranging from Internet publishing and telephony to the latest flavors of "push computing," which has become a hot new Internet business.

Conference executive producer David Coursey said among the roughly 60 demonstrations over the three days will be new implementations using Java, the programming language developed by Sun Microsystems Inc..

"You'll see some interesting Java startups," Coursey said ahead of the conference, noting products will range from building programs to showing animation on pages that can be displayed using the Internet's World Wide Web.

Since Java was launched two years ago, the programming language has been much ballyhooed as a technology which can bring the promise of eventually allowing one piece of software to run on otherwise incompatible computers.
But only recently has the software become sufficiently extensive for companies to be building major software products using the language itself.
Internet telephony will also be a focus, Coursey said.
"I'm talking about everything from a better phone that you can use at home to access the Internet to companies that are going to do telephony-based services," he said.

An Intel representative said the company will show a variety of initiatives ranging from ways of combining compact disks with Internet updates to Java tools and new entertainment capabilities using personal computers.
Publishers will get a chance to view two systems for publishing over the Internet, including one International Business Machines Corp. is due to bring to market.

Although the Internet is often touted as a means to enable everyone to become a publisher, these products are expected to come with a hefty price tag which is geared for serious business publishing on the Web.

Coursey said in addition to big name presenters, but also a healthy number of new startup companies of the size which a year ago might have raced into the public market but are now seeking corporate alliances.
"The happy thing is return of the garage shop - the return of two people in a garage building companies," he said, a reference to Silicon Valley style entrepreneurs.
"You're going to see some of these 10-11 person company, that are big enough to now have the first generation of their products but are still very small."

The final day of the conference on Wednesday will showcase companies offering so-called push technologies, which can automatically deliver software or information to people's computer screens over networks or the Internet.

"Almost everyone is trying to find a way to somehow be a push company," said Coursey, although he also noted the term has become so over-used in the last four months that "people are beginning to recoil from the term."
PointCast virtually single-handedly defined the category a year ago with its advertising-supported automatically-updating screen saver information service.

Last week, the company said it has signed up more than 1,000 companies to broadcast information using its software, including a deal with Excite Inc to build a directory for sifting through new channels.

More than 30 firms have jumped into push computing, many of whom will be showing products on this final day, sponsored by Tibco, a unit of Reuters Holdings Plc, the worldwide news and information company. ((sam.perry@reuters.com, Palo Alto Bureau 415 846 5400))
